Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Specify the pathophysiology of risk factors for, and treatment options for knee arthrofibrosis.
Understand the appropriate workup and imaging studies for the diagnosis of aseptic
loosening.
Understand the pathophysiology and treatment options for polyethylene wear and osteolysis.
Recognize the signs of metal hypersensitivity and understand appropriate diagnostic tests and
treatment options for metal hypersensitivity.
Arthrofibrosis
Background

Stiffness after total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is common and multifactorial.
Arthrofibrosis is a pathologic condition characterized by diffuse scar tissue formation.

Background
TKA can afford effective pain relief and improve patient function. To achieve these goals,
appropriate implant fixation and positioning, ligamentous stability, and adequate range
of motion (ROM) are essential. However, postoperative stiffness is common after TKA.
Multiple factors, including infection, component malrotation or malalignment, improper
component sizing, complex regional pain syndrome, and heterotopic ossification, may
lead to stiffness. Arthrofibrosis, a pathologic condition characterized by diffuse
periarticular scar tissue formation, also may cause painful joint stiffness.1,2
Arthrofibrosis may occur secondary to injury, infection, or hemarthrosis or may be
idiopathic in nature. Often, a diagnosis of exclusion, arthrofibrosis is established after
infectious, mechanical, and technical factors have been ruled out.
Although no consensus exists with regard to the definition of stiffness after TKA, it has
been described as inadequate ROM leading to functional limitations in activities of daily
living.3 Traditionally, a minimum postoperative ROM of 0° to 110° was considered a
successful outcome.4 Currently, stiffness after TKA is defined as 10° of extension or less,
less than 80° to 110° of flexion, decreased motion compared with preoperative status,
and patient dissatisfaction with ROM.2 Gait analysis demonstrates that patients require
67° of knee flexion to walk, 90° to 100° of knee flexion to use stairs, and 105° of knee
flexion to rise from a low chair.5 Minor losses in knee extension increase energy
expenditure during gait, may lead to quadriceps fatigue during the stance phase of gait,
and may limit activities of daily living. Arthrofibrosis is a specific diagnosis made after
infectious and mechanical factors have been ruled out.
Epidemiology
Wide range in reported stiffness after TKA
Approximately 4% of patients who undergo TKA are affected by arthrofibrosis postoperatively.


Epidemiology
No consensus exists with regard to the definition of arthrofibrosis of the knee after TKA,
complicating determination of its true prevalence. In addition, confusion exists in the
literature with regard to the terms stiffness, arthrofibrosis, and flexion contracture,
which often are used interchangeably. Rates of postoperative knee stiffness range from
zero to 54%.2,6,7 A recent systematic review and meta-analysis examined 35 studies and
reported that the rate of arthrofibrosis was 4% after primary TKA.6
Pathophysiology
Arthrofibrosis involves proliferation of collagen and extracellular matrix.
Several cytokines and growth factors are involved, including interleukin (IL)-1, IL-6, tumor
necrosis factor-alpha, transforming growth factor-beta, platelet-derived growth factor, and
bone morphogenic protein-2.

Pathophysiology
Arthrofibrosis is a fibrosing disorder of the synovial membrane and periarticular soft
tissues. The pathophysiology of arthrofibrosis is incompletely understood but involves
the aberrant proliferation of collagen, extracellular matrix, and often heterotopic bone
within the joint and adjacent soft tissues. Several cytokines and growth factors are
involved in the pathogenesis of arthrofibrosis, including IL-1, IL-6, tumor necrosis factor-
alpha, transforming growth factor-beta, platelet-derived growth factor, and bone
morphogenic protein-2.8
Risk Factors
Multiple risk factors for arthrofibrosis include prior surgery and poor preoperative motion.


Risk Factors
The etiology of arthrofibrosis is unclear; however, several patient characteristics and
factors have been shown to increase the risk of postoperative stiffness. Poor
preoperative ROM is the strongest predictor for poor motion after TKA. Prior surgery,
complex primary arthroplasty, and a genetic linkage have been associated with
postoperative arthrofibrosis.1,9
Evaluation
Patient History and Diagnosis
The diagnosis of arthrofibrosis is one of exclusion.
Other more common causes of stiffness must be ruled out before a diagnosis of arthrofibrosis
is made.

Patient History and Diagnosis
A diagnosis of arthrofibrosis is made only after all other causes of stiffness have been
ruled out, including mechanical and infectious etiologies. Documentation of preoperative
ROM and prior knee surgery can help identify patient risk factors (eg, did the patient
have adequate ROM and then regress, or did poor motion occur early postoperatively). A
detailed patient history also may aid in diagnosis (eg, an infectious history should include
the presence of constitutional symptoms and any wound healing complications). Basic
laboratory screening tests, including C-reactive protein level and erythrocyte
sedimentation rate should be performed; any abnormalities in these laboratory values
should prompt joint aspiration.
Physical Examination

The physical examination includes evaluation for any signs of infection, measuring ROM,
determining coronal and sagittal stability, and assessing the soft tissues and patellar mobility.

Physical Examination
The physical examination begins with a detailed inspection of the incision for erythema,
swelling, draining sinus, scar widening or hypertrophy, and skin hypomobility. A
complete neurovascular examination of the limb, including ipsilateral hip examination, is
performed because knee pain and stiffness may be associated with hip arthritis. ROM
should be measured with the use of a goniometer. Knee stability should be examined to
varus and valgus stress, and anterior and posterior drawer tests should be performed.
These tests should be performed with the knee in extension and 90° of flexion.
Although the concept may seem counterintuitive, instability may lead to pain and
subsequent stiffness. For example, flexion instability can promote abnormal kinematics
that cause pain in the pericapsular tissues, ultimately leading to stiffness. The examiner
also should assess patellar tracking and the foot progression angle. Malrotation of the
components, especially internal rotation of the tibial component, may lead to external
rotation of the foot and patellar maltracking. In this scenario, a patient may present with
a stiff and painful knee. In addition, lack of passive motion of the patella may
differentiate the underlying cause and indicate arthrofibrosis. If the patella cannot be
passively mobilized and the anterior tissues are thickened, then a diagnosis of
arthrofibrosis is more likely.
Imaging Studies
Radiographs of the knee may reveal implant loosening, component malpositioning, and
incorrect sizing.
The threshold for imaging the ipsilateral hip should be low.
CT can be performed to rule out malrotation. If CT is ordered, detailed instructions and the
reason for the test should be provided to the technologist and radiologist.


Imaging Studies
Plain radiographs are first imaging study obtained to determine implant fixation. For
cemented and noncemented TKA implants, good quality radiographs obtained tangential
to the implants are paramount for visualizing the bone-implant interface and assessing
for radiolucency. Comparison with prior radiographs may reveal the progression of
radiolucencies and any changes in implant position. If the implant appears well fixed, it
should be evaluated for any technical errors because these may lead to stiffness after
TKA. Technical errors include malpositioned or oversized components, flexion and
extension gap imbalances, joint line alteration, incorrect tibial slope, poor reconstruction
of the patellofemoral joint, and failure to restore posterior condylar offset. Sagittal plane
component positioning should be measured because abnormalities may cause
restrictions in motion. Although MRI can detect fibrous proliferation and some centers
have found MRI useful in assessing for osteolysis, MRI has no role in the diagnosis of
arthrofibrosis after TKA.
Internal rotation of the tibia, the femur, or both may lead to a painful and ultimately stiff
knee. If plain radiographs do not reveal this diagnosis, CT can be performed to assess
the rotational positioning of the tibial and femoral components. However, measuring
rotation on CT scans may be a challenge; therefore, care must be taken to ensure
accurate replication. If all these mechanical causes have been ruled out, a diagnosis of
arthrofibrosis is favored.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Early, aggressive physical therapy is the main treatment option.
Physical therapy should focus on control of pain and inflammation and should emphasize
ROM over strengthening.

Nonsurgical Management
SEND FEEDBACK

A supervised or self-guided physical therapy regimen is important for recovery after
primary TKA. In patients with stiffness in the early postoperative period, the emphasis
should be on pain control, management of inflammation, frequent monitoring, and ROM
rather than aggressive strengthening. Early physical therapy and adequate pain control
after TKA have been shown to decrease the rate of future arthrofibrosis.4 In a Danish
study, preoperative patient education substantially decreased the risk of postoperative
stiffness requiring manipulation under anesthesia (MUA) and should be strongly
considered in patients with relevant risk factors.10
Manipulation Under Anesthesia
MUA is a first-line nonsurgical treatment option.
Intervention should be performed less than 3 months after primary TKA.

Manipulation Under Anesthesia
If knee ROM does not improve with physical therapy, MUA typically is a first-line
treatment option. The most common MUA technique involves general anesthesia and a
combination of hip and knee flexion. The hip is flexed to 90° while the proximal tibia is
held. The knee is gently flexed and extended through the proximal tibia until a palpable
and audible lysis of adhesions is appreciated. This process may take several minutes
because of the plastic deformation of the scar tissues. Pre-manipulation and post-
manipulation ROM should be accurately recorded.2 Figure 1 shows the proper
technique for MUA.

Figure 1 Clinical photographs show range of motion before and after manipulation.
Improvement in range of motion from before manipulation (left image) to after

A systematic review reported a mean improvement in ROM of 38.4° and a mean increase
of 29.4° of flexion after MUA.11 The timing of MUA is a subject of debate in the literature,
but most studies agree that performing MUA less than 3 months after TKA is
appropriate. In assessing the benefits of MUA, potential complications, including
fracture, wound dehiscence, patellar tendon/quadriceps tendon strain or rupture, and
hemarthrosis, also should be considered.

Lysis of Adhesions
Arthroscopic and open lysis of adhesions are options for restoring motion after TKA.
Both have limited indications but have demonstrated success according to the literature.

Lysis of Adhesions
If previous treatment options, including MUA, have failed to restore motion and more
than 3 months have passed since TKA, arthroscopic or open lysis of adhesions may be
considered. In a retrospective study, the reported incidence of lysis of adhesions to
manage all-cause stiffness after TKA was 0.8%.12
Arthroscopic lysis of adhesions is less invasive than open lysis of adhesions and focuses
on resection of fibrous tissue in the suprapatellar pouch, medial/lateral gutters, and
intercondylar groove and release/recession of the posterior cruciate ligament, if
necessary. Studies on the arthroscopic lysis of adhesions in combination with MUA have
demonstrated flexion improvement of 24° to 34°, extension increase of 12° to 23°, and
an overall increase of 24° to 31° of motion.7,9
Open lysis of adhesions typically is recommended if ROM is severely limited or a severe
flexion deformity precludes arthroscopy. Mean improvement in overall knee ROM is 39°
with open lysis of adhesions.7,9 During an open procedure, the polyethylene should be
exchanged to access the posterior knee. Meticulous débridement and scar resection of
the posteromedial corner, posterior capsule, suprapatellar pouch, and medial/lateral
gutters also should be performed.
Risks associated with both procedures include damage to the prosthesis, infection,
hemarthrosis, extensor mechanism injury, fracture, and neurovascular injury. Because
the gains in ROM after arthroscopic and open lysis of adhesions are similar to those after
MUA, the utility of these interventions is limited, and they are not routinely performed.
Revision TKA

9/32

Revision TKA is most effective in correcting mechanical errors associated with stiffness after
TKA.
Patients with a diagnosis of arthrofibrosis demonstrate the lowest gain in motion after revision
TKA but do demonstrate improvements in pain.
Recurrent stiffness is the most common complication after revision TKA for stiffness.

Revision TKA
In patients with refractory stiffness after TKA that does not respond to other treatment
modalities, revision TKA is an option. Revision TKA is thought to be most effective for
correction of mechanical errors, such as improper component sizing, malpositioning of
components, joint line alteration, and overstuffing of the patellofemoral joint.13 A
systematic review of revision TKA outcomes demonstrated a mean ROM of 40° to 72°
preoperatively and improvement to 68° to 98° postoperatively. The mean gain in ROM
was 30°, with the mean flexion contracture decreasing by 10° to 4° postoperatively.
Patients with a diagnosis of arthrofibrosis and no underlying mechanical etiology for
stiffness had the smallest improvement in ROM after revision TKA but did report
improvement with respect to pain.14 However, arthrofibrosis is prone to recurrence and
is a leading cause of re-revision for stiffness; in two studies, more than 25% of patients
who underwent revision TKAs for stiffness required a second revision procedure.13,14
Other complications include persistent pain, component loosening, infection, tendon
rupture, nerve palsy, and fracture (Resource 1).
Aseptic Loosening
Overview
Aseptic loosening is the most common reason for late revision after TKA.
Causes of aseptic loosening include mechanical loosening, osteolysis, and instability.
According to several follow-up studies, aseptic loosening after TKA is the most common cause
of late failure and revision.15-17 Aseptic loosening has several causes.
Mechanical loosening
The main mechanism is micromotion at the implant-bone interface.

Poor bone-cement interdigitation may lead to subsidence and loosening.
Additional factors that may lead to loosening include inaccurate bone cuts, poor
cementation technique, and deficient/osteoporotic bone.
Osteolysis related to wear particles and debris (secondary to polyethylene wear, metal and
cement particles)
Malpositioning of components and tibiofemoral malalignment leads to increased stress loads
on the tibial component and polyethylene.
Earlier implant designs with less conformity and/or less fixation may have been less
forgiving for malalignment, leading to higher failure rates. Current designs tend to have
more conformity and better fixation technology and may tolerate some varus/valgus
malalignment without increased risk of failure.
Instability leads to inappropriate articulation and increased focal stresses on the implant and
subsequent loosening.
Evaluation
Patient History and Physical Examination
Aseptic loosening typically presents after the knee replacement has functioned well for a
period
The patient examination should attempt to rule out infection and identify any instability.

Patient History and Physical Examination
Patients with aseptic loosening commonly present with pain and instability that worsens
with weight bearing and improves with rest; aseptic loosening frequently is associated
with startup pain. Timing and duration of symptoms are important. Patients with loose
implants frequently experience a well-functioning knee for a period before symptom
manifestation. An infection should be ruled out, with erythrocyte sedimentation rate and
C-reactive protein level obtained before planned revision. Ligamentous stability should
be assessed with a focus on collateral ligament integrity. The tibial component is most
often affected by aseptic loosening. Video 1 summarizes the work up and physical
examination of patients with a painful TKA implant. Resource 2 highlights a

Imaging Studies
Serial radiographs are standard imaging study for monitoring prosthetic loosening.
Implant zones are classified according to the Modern Knee Society Radiographic Evaluation
System.
Bone scans are nonspecific and infrequently recommended.

Imaging Studies
Serial radiographs are recommended for interval comparison of radiolucent lines and
component positioning. Standard radiographs include a weight-bearing AP view, true
lateral view with the knee in 30° of flexion, and patellofemoral view. The fixation
interface of all implants should be examined for radiolucent lines on AP, lateral, and

patellofemoral views. The implant zones are classified according to the Modern Knee
Society Radiographic Evaluation System18 (Figure 2). Criteria for loosening include
radiolucent lines larger than 2 mm or progressively enlarging prosthesis-cement or
bone-cement radiolucent lines, component migration, subsidence, cement fracture, or
change in tibiofemoral alignment on weight-bearing views. With noncemented TKA
implants, displaced porous-coated beads, called bead shedding, are an additional
finding. Loosening of the femoral component is more difficult to detect; therefore, a true
lateral view of the component must be obtained to evaluate for any radiolucent lines.
Oblique views may help detect radiolucent lines around the posterior femoral condyles.
Bone scans are of limited utility in TKA because they will demonstrate increased uptake
for several years postoperatively as a result of normal bone remodeling, leading to a
high rate of false-positive results.19

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Asymptomatic patients with signs of loosening may be monitored.
Follow-up radiographs are recommended.

Nonsurgical Management
Asymptomatic patients with radiographic signs of loosening but no signs of component
migration may be monitored. Routine follow-up with serial radiographs is necessary to
monitor component positioning and stability. Earlier follow-up and reevaluation are
warranted with any change in symptoms or stability of the knee.
Surgical Management
Symptomatic patients with loose implants are candidates for revision TKA.
Surgical goals include correcting the underlying cause of failure and providing stable
component fixation.
Multiple options exist for fixation, including stems, porous sleeves and cones, and allograft.

Surgical Management
In patients with symptomatic loosening, the goals of revision surgery include addressing
the underlying cause of component failure, such as malrotation or malalignment, and
achieving joint stability with adequate fixation. Intraoperative bone loss is classified
according the Anderson Orthopaedic Research Institute system20 (Table 1). In patients
with aseptic loosening and bone loss, a stepwise progression should be followed to

to proper rotation and to the femoral component if revised. Stems have demonstrated
increased survivorship in revision TKA, and their use should be considered.21 Porous
metaphyseal cones and sleeves are a modern option to manage bone loss. They provide
biologic fixation, can fill large defects, and provide immediate structural support.22 Long-
term outcomes after revision TKA for aseptic loosening include good survivorship and
function23 (Resource 3).

Polyethylene Wear and Osteolysis
Overview
Historically, polyethylene wear was a leading cause of TKA failure; however, failure rates have
decreased with improved materials.
Polyethylene wear is the main cause of osteolysis.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:43 AM
AAOS | Complications After Total Knee Arthroplasty: Other
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001036
15/32


Overview
Historically, polyethylene wear was a leading cause of TKA failure.17 However, more
recent studies have demonstrated a notable decrease in late revision procedures for
polyethylene wear (ie, >40% in 2002 to 4.3% in 2012).15 Reduced wear and revision rates
are attributed to advances in the design and manufacturing of polyethylene.
Despite device improvements, polyethylene wear is the main cause of osteolysis.
Accumulation of polyethylene particles in the joint activate several cell lines of adaptive
and innate immunity. Treatment options for osteolytic lesions range from polyethylene
exchange and intralesional bone grafting to revision with distal stem fixation, porous
metal sleeves or cones, and varying levels of knee constraint based on the integrity of
the ligaments and periarticular soft tissues.
Evolution of Polyethylene
Changes in the manufacturing of polyethylene have substantially improved wear properties.
Remelting and annealing of polyethylene decrease free radicals and subsequent oxidation but
worsen its mechanical characteristics.

Evolution of Polyethylene
The science and manufacturing of polyethylene has undergone major advancements. To
prevent oxidation, gamma sterilization of ultra-high–molecular-weight polyethylene in air
of has transitioned to sterilization in inert gases (ie, gas plasma, ethylene oxide).
Remaining free radicals are removed via remelting or annealing of the polyethylene.
Although remelting is more effective at removing free radicals, it decreases the ductility
of polyethylene, diminishing its mechanical properties, and increases the risk of fracture.
Prior generations of polyethylene were packaged in air, allowing for implant oxidation on
the shelf. Currently, implants typically are vacuum packaged. Highly cross-linked
polyethylene also is produced via higher levels of irradiation. The cross-linking confers
better wear properties and has demonstrated superior wear characteristics in total hip

9/3/26, 7:43 AM
AAOS | Complications After Total Knee Arthroplasty: Other
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001036
16/32

arthroplasty (THA). Newer generations also use infused vitamin E to combat oxidation.
However, the use of highly cross-linked polyethylene and vitamin E–infused polyethylene
in TKA remains controversial; although outcomes are similar to those of conventional
ultra-high–molecular-weight polyethylene, the costs are higher with the newer
technology.24,25
Wear and Osteolysis
The pattern of polyethylene wear in TKA differs from that in THA. Pitting and delamination are
observed on the polyethylene/femoral articulation after TKA, and adhesive and abrasive wear
patterns are observed on the backside of polyethylene in modular tibial components.

Wear and Osteolysis
The bearing surface of the knee has a different wear mechanism than that of the hip.
Pitting and delamination are observed because of sliding, rolling, and rotational
movements after TKA. With modular tibial trays, backside wear also occurs,
demonstrating an adhesive and abrasive wear pattern. In THA implants, wear particles
generally are smaller than in TKA implants because of the difference in mechanisms, and
the wear particles in THA implants are more reactive. Macrophages readily absorb these
wear particles, releasing cytokines. The predominant feature of osteolysis is release of
receptor activator nuclear factor-κ B ligand and activation of osteoclast bone resorption.
An elevated level of receptor activator nuclear factor-κ B ligand leads to osteolysis and
subsequent bone loss.25 Conversely, polyethylene wear is influenced by patient factors,
such as age, body mass index, and activity level. Deviations from optimal alignment may
lead to localized increases in contact pressure and increased wear rates. Rotating-
platform inserts are associated with lower rates of backside wear, but rates of
tibiofemoral wear are similar to those of fixed-bearing inserts. Insert thickness should be
greater or equal to 8 mm to prevent excessive wear or catastrophic failure24 (Resource
4).

Evaluation
Patient History and Physical Examination
Osteolysis frequently is asymptomatic and often is observed incidentally in routine
radiographs.
The initial patient evaluation should focus on ruling out infection.

Patient History and Physical Examination
Wear-induced osteolysis frequently is asymptomatic and often is identified on routine
follow-up radiographs. Symptomatic patients with osteolysis may present with pain,
recurrent effusions, or late instability associated with the polyethylene wear. A detailed
patient history should examine the timing and onset of pain. Frequently, patients with
wear and osteolysis report a previously well-functioning implant with late onset of
mechanical symptoms and pain. The initial evaluation should focus on ruling out
infection, with laboratory studies performed as indicated. A focused knee examination
should evaluate for areas of tenderness or instability.
Imaging Studies
Polyethylene wear may be difficult to appreciate on radiographs.
Advanced imaging studies, including CT scans or MRIs, are useful for characterizing and
assessing osteolysis.

Imaging Studies
On weight-bearing plain radiographs, wear may be observed with narrowing of the
prosthetic joint spaces. If wear is asymmetric, varus or valgus deformity or patellar tilt
may occur (Figure 3). Mild liner wear may be difficult to appreciate because of
differences in patient positioning between radiographs.

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Serial radiographs and monitoring of clinical symptoms are acceptable for the management of
small osteolytic lesions.
Changes in symptoms and an increase in pain require repeated imaging studies and follow-up.

Nonsurgical Management
For patients with osteolytic lesions smaller than1 cm and no clinical symptoms,
radiographic monitoring (ie, serial radiographs) is acceptable. No consensus exists with
regard to the lesion size that warrants surgical management versus continued
monitoring. Indications for surgical management are multifactorial, depending on the

location and rate of progression of the lesion, component stability, and the risk of
component failure or periprosthetic fracture with continued observation.
Surgical Management
Surgical management for well-fixed components may involve removal of the offending
polyethylene and bone grafting for small osteolytic lesions. If these lesions are large, revision
TKA is necessary.
Loose implants with bone loss require component revision with reconstruction.
Multiple revision options exist, including stems, porous sleeves and cones, and allograft.

Surgical Management
Small osteolytic lesions around well-fixed components can be managed via intralesional
débridement, bone grafting, and polyethylene exchange. However, this requires an
appropriately aligned, well-balanced knee with intact ligaments. In this treatment option,
defects accessed through a peripheral cortical window. No consensus exists with regard
to the lesion size that is appropriate for this treatment option; however, patients with
lesions that are larger, symptomatic, progressive, at risk of fracture, or associated with
loose implants should undergo revision TKA, because more complex reconstruction is
required. Metaphyseal bone defects and larger, contained defects require distal stem
fixation, structural allograft, or porous sleeves or cones.22 Given the promising
outcomes of porous sleeves and cones in recent studies, the use of structural allograft
has decreased (Resource 5).
Goals of surgical management include proper management of bone loss to restore a
stable implant and proper limb alignment. Therefore, the collateral ligaments and
epicondyles should be closely examined. In patients with any collateral ligament
insufficiency, constrained prostheses should be used.

Overview
Metal hypersensitivity is a controversial topic.
The most common sensitizing metal is nickel.
Patch testing is unreliable in the diagnosis of metal hypersensitivity in a patient with a painful
TKA implant.

Overview
In the last several years, allergy and metal hypersensitivities have gained prominence as
explanations for persistent pain and dissatisfaction after TKA. Metal ions released from
TKA components may form complexes with native proteins, which may act as antigens or
allergens and cause an immunologic response in a synovial joint or elsewhere in the
body. The most common metal sensitizer is nickel, followed by cobalt and chromium.
Studies have reported an increasing prevalence of patch tests positive for metal after
TKA. However, even if local and systemic exposure to metals indicates sensitization, a
positive patch test result does not confirm metal hypersensitivity as the cause of a
painful TKA implant.
Pathophysiology
Hypersensitivity to a metal implant is a type IV allergic response.
Although the exact mechanism of this response is unknown, it differs from a cutaneous
reaction.

Pathophysiology
Metal ions can be released via corrosion or mechanical processes, such as wear.
Implant-related hypersensitivity is a type IV allergic response, a delayed cell-mediated
response with activation of specific T lymphocytes. Lymphocytes release various
cytokines, activating a response that leads to inflammation and eventual periprosthetic

unknown, but the process is distinct from a cutaneous response.
Epidemiology
10% to 15% of the general population has a metal sensitivity.
In patients with poorly functioning implants, the prevalence ranges from 13% to 70%.

Epidemiology
Ten percent to 15% of the general population has a metal sensitivity. In patients with
loose, failed, or poorly functioning implants, metal sensitivity ranges from 13% to 70%.28
Whether this sensitivity is the cause of implant malfunction or an effect of implant
malfunction is unknown.29 A positive patch test result has not been shown to be
substantially associated with implant failure.30 In 2014, a study of Australian
Arthroplasty Registry data indicated that 1.8% of all TKA revision procedures were
performed because of metal-related pathology.31
Evaluation
Patient History, Physical Examination, and Initial Workup
Metal hypersensitivity is a subject of controversy and debate.
The diagnosis is one of exclusion, and all other potential causes must be ruled out.
Infection is the first diagnosis to be ruled out.

Patient History, Physical Examination, and Initial Workup
Metal hypersensitivity is a very rare and controversial diagnosis and remains a diagnosis
of exclusion. Painful synovitis after TKA typically is related to infection, instability,
loosening, polyethylene wear and osteolysis, or recurrent hemarthrosis. The most

Less frequently, eczematous dermatitis is described. Patient presentation often is vague
and nonspecific and may be indistinguishable from that of an indolent infection. The
development of cutaneous symptoms after TKA is rare and does not correlate with a
preoperative diagnosis of contact dermatitis to components of the implants. A history of
infections should be elicited, with infection being the first diagnosis ruled out. The
minimum laboratory workup should include C-reactive protein level, erythrocyte
sedimentation rate, and knee joint aspiration if indicated. Cultures should be held for 2
weeks to identify potentially slow-growing organisms. Serum metal ion levels are of little
diagnostic utility because they may be elevated in patients with a well-functioning TKA
implant.
Imaging Studies
Plain radiographs are first-line imaging studies. Advanced imaging studies have limited utility
in the diagnosis of metal hypersensitivity.

Imaging Studies
Plain radiographs should be obtained to identify a mechanical source of pain and signs
of osteolysis or implant loosening. If concern for osteolysis exists, CT can be performed
to further characterize any lesions.
Testing
Testing options include cutaneous patch testing and lymphocyte transformation testing.
These tests are limited by specificity and sensitivity for subsequent patient reactions to the
metal implants.

No generally accepted and reliable tests are available for the diagnosis of metal
hypersensitivity after TKA. Patch testing is frequently used to diagnose contact allergy to
metals, but it is unclear how the results relate to hypersensitivity to a TKA implant given
the differences in mechanisms. Figure 6 shows a mild allergic response to nickel with
cutaneous patch testing (upper left box of panel 1). The most common blood test for
metal sensitivity after TKA is lymphocyte transformation, in which a patient’s blood
lymphocytes and monocytes are challenged via a variety of metal salts. Radioactive
nucleotide uptake by the lymphocytes and monocytes is then measured, with increased
uptake demonstrating prior sensitivity to a particular metal. This test is limited by cost,
availability, and specificity and sensitivity with respect to patient disease. No evidence
supports preoperative allergy testing in patients with a reported metal allergy.

Management
Nonsurgical Management
No effective nonsurgical treatment options exist for the management of metal hypersensitivity
associated with TKA.

Nonsurgical Management
Treatment of patients with a suspected metal hypersensitivity is poorly defined, with no
proven nonsurgical treatment options available. Anecdotal reports suggest that topical
steroids are effective in treating eczematous reactions.
Surgical Management
Revision surgery is a last resort treatment option for the management of metal
hypersensitivity.
Revision surgery is performed to replace the offending implant with a hypoallergenic implant
(chosen from various available devices).

Surgical Management
If revision surgery is considered after TKA implant failure, proper diagnosis of the failure
is paramount. Revision based on pain alone may lead to a poor outcome. The diagnosis

the offending prostheses and replacement with hypoallergenic implants.
Two main categories of implants are currently available:
Cobalt-chromium implants coated with hypoallergenic materials, such as titanium
nitride, zirconium nitride, or zirconium oxide
Implants made from other materials, such as all-ceramic, oxidized zirconium, pure
titanium, and all-polyethylene tibial components.28,32
Small case series and case reports have demonstrated satisfactory outcomes after
revision with hypoallergenic implants. However, no evidence-based guidelines on use of
these implants have been published. Resources 6 and 7 provide a good overview of the
available literature, diagnosis, and treatment options associated with metal
